A rare hormonal disorder characterized by abnormal enlargement of the extremities (hands and feet) caused by the excessive secretion of growth hormone after puberty. Contrast with gigantism.

A potentially life-threatening condition that occurs when the adrenal glands do not produce enough of the hormones cortisol or aldosterone. Characterized by chronic, worsening fatigue and muscle weakness; loss of appetite; low blood pressure; and weight loss. Many patients also develop patches of dark skin.
Inflammation of one or both of the adrenal glands. Autoimmune adrenalitis is the most common cause of Addison's disease.
An abnormality of the electrolyte balance that is caused by the excessive secretion of aldosterone. The primary symptom is high blood pressure.

Abbreviated ADH; secreted by the hypothalamus and stored in the pituitary gland. Helps control blood pressure by reducing the amount of water that is excreted through the kidneys. In contrast, a diuretic is administered to increase the amount of urine secretion.
A hormone produced by the thyroid gland that works with the parathyroid hormone to decrease calcium levels in the blood and tissues by moving calcium into storage in the bones and teeth.
The steroid hormones produced by the adrenal cortex. The same term describes synthetically produced equivalents that are administered as medications.
Also known as hydrocortisone; a corticosteroid that has an anti-inflammatory action. Also helps regulate the metabolism of carbohydrates, fats, and proteins in the body.
A congenital form of hypothyroidism. If thyroid hormone replacement is not started soon after birth, causes arrested physical and mental development.

Also known as hypercortisolism; caused by prolonged exposure to high levels of cortisol. Signs include a rounded, red moon face. Can be caused by overproduction of cortisol by the body or by prolonged use of corticosteroids.

Abbreviated DI; not related to diabetes mellitus. An uncommon disorder caused by an insufficient production of the antidiuretic hormone ADH or by the inability of the kidneys to respond appropriately to this hormone. Causes an imbalance of fluids in the body, leading to extreme thirst and frequent urination.

Abbreviated DM; the most common endocrine system disease. A group of metabolic disorders characterized by hyperglycemia resulting from defects in the body's production of insulin (type 1) or its ability to use it properly (type 2). Not related to diabetes insipidus.

Abbreviated DKA; a life-threatening diabetes complication caused by a buildup of acids (called ketones) in the blood. Treatment includes the administration of insulin and the replacement of fluids and electrolytes.

Damage to the retina as a complication of uncontrolled diabetes. Occurs when diabetes damages the tiny blood vessels in the retina, causing blood to leak into the posterior segment of the eyeball and producing the damage that causes the loss of vision.
Mineral substances (calcium, chloride, magnesium, phosphorus, sodium, and potassium) that are normally found in the blood and other bodily fluids.

Abbreviated Epi or EPI; also known as adrenaline. Stimulates the sympathetic nervous system in response to physical injury or to mental stress such as fear. Makes the heart beat faster and can raise blood pressure; also helps the liver release glucose and limits the release of insulin.
Abbreviated E; a hormone secreted by the ovaries that is important for the development and maintenance of the female secondary sex characteristics and in regulation of the menstrual cycle.
An abnormal protrusion of the eyeball out of the orbit.

definition: Abbreviated FSH; stimulates the secretion of estrogen and the growth of ova (eggs) in the ovaries of the female. In the male, it stimulates the production of sperm in the testicles (testes).
A blood test that measures average glucose levels over the previous 3 weeks. Able to detect changes more rapidly than the HbA1c test.

Abbreviated GDM; a form of diabetes mellitus that occurs during some pregnancies, affecting approximately 2–10% of pregnancies in the United States. Usually resolves after delivery; however, these women have an increased risk of developing type 2 diabetes later in life.
Abnormal growth of the entire body that is caused by excessive secretion of growth hormone before puberty. Contrast with acromegaly.

Abbreviated GCG; the hormone secreted by the alpha cells of the pancreatic islets in response to low levels of glucose in the bloodstream. Increases the glucose level by stimulating the liver to convert glycogen into glucose for release into the bloodstream. Can be administered via injection for severe hypoglycemia if the person is unable to take glucose by mouth.
The basic form of energy used by the body. Glucose in the bloodstream is also known as blood sugar.

Abbreviated GD; a disorder of unknown cause in which the immune system attacks the thyroid gland and stimulates it to make excessive amounts of thyroid hormone. Results in hyperthyroidism and can also cause goiter, exophthalmos, or both. The most common cause of hyperthyroidism.
Abbreviated GH; also known as the somatotropic hormone. Regulates the growth of bone, muscle, and other body tissues.
The condition of excessive mammary development in the male. Caused by an increase in male estrogen levels or a decrease in testosterone.

definition: Also known as Hashimoto's thyroiditis; an autoimmune disease in which the body's own antibodies attack and destroy the cells of the thyroid gland. This inflammation often leads to hypothyroidism.

Abnormally high concentrations of calcium circulating in the blood instead of being stored in the bones and teeth. Can lead to weakened bones and the formation of kidney stones. Hypercalcemia is the opposite of hypocalcemia.
breakdown_text: hyper-: excessive ; calc: calcium ; -emia: blood condition

definition: An abnormally high concentration of glucose in the blood. Seen primarily in patients with diabetes mellitus; symptoms include polydipsia, polyphagia, and polyuria. Hyperglycemia is the opposite of hypoglycemia.
breakdown_text: hyper-: excessive ; glyc: sugar ; -emia: blood condition

definition: The condition of excessive secretion of insulin in the bloodstream. Can cause hypoglycemia.
The excess secretion of growth hormone that causes both acromegaly and gigantism. Usually caused by a pituitary adenoma.

Also known as thyrotoxicosis; the overproduction of thyroid hormones, which causes an imbalance of metabolism. Symptoms include an increased metabolic rate, sweating, nervousness, and weight loss. The most common cause is Graves' disease.

An abnormally low concentration of glucose (sugar) in the blood. Symptoms include nervousness and shakiness, confusion, perspiration, or feeling anxious or weak. Hypoglycemia is the opposite of hyperglycemia.
breakdown_text: hypo-: deficient ; glyc: sugar ; -emia: blood condition

definition: Also known as an underactive thyroid; a condition caused by a deficiency of thyroid secretion. Symptoms include fatigue, depression, sensitivity to cold, and a decreased metabolic rate.

The hormone secreted by the beta cells of the pancreatic islets in response to high levels of glucose in the bloodstream. When energy is needed, it allows glucose to enter the cells to be used as energy; when additional glucose is not needed, it stimulates the liver to convert glucose into glycogen for storage.
A benign tumor of the pancreas that secretes additional insulin, causing hypoglycemia (low blood glucose).

A normal metabolic process that helps the body utilize stored fat when other sources of energy are lacking. An excessively high level may indicate that the body is not producing enough insulin to convert glucose into energy. A ketogenic diet, which is high in fat and low in carbohydrates, has been shown to be helpful in managing epileptic seizures.
A minimally invasive surgical procedure to remove one or both adrenal glands.

A hormone secreted by fat cells that is involved in the regulation of appetite. Travels in the bloodstream to the brain, where it acts on the hypothalamus to suppress appetite and burn fat stored in adipose tissue.
Abbreviated LH; stimulates ovulation in the female. In the male, stimulates the secretion of testosterone.
Also known as adult hypothyroidism; caused by an extreme deficiency of thyroid secretion. Symptoms include swelling, particularly around the eyes and cheeks, fatigue, and a subnormal temperature.

Both a hormone and a neurohormone; released as a hormone by the adrenal medulla and as a neurohormone by the sympathetic nervous system. Plays an important role in the fight-or-flight response by raising blood pressure, strengthening the heartbeat, and stimulating muscle contractions.

Abbreviated OXT; stimulates uterine contractions during childbirth. After childbirth, controls postnatal hemorrhage and stimulates the flow of milk from the mammary glands. Pitocin is a synthetic form administered to induce or speed up labor.
An inflammation of the pancreas. Alcohol abuse is a leading cause.
The surgical removal of one or more of the parathyroid glands, performed to control hyperparathyroidism or remove parathyroid tumors.

Also known as a pituitary tumor; a slow-growing benign tumor of the pituitary gland. Functional pituitary tumors often produce hormones in large and unregulated amounts, which might include ACTH, growth hormones, prolactin, or TSH.
Excessive thirst.
Excessive hunger.
Excessive urination.

A condition in which the blood glucose level is higher than normal, but not high enough to be classified as type 2 diabetes. Indicates an increased risk of developing type 2 diabetes, heart disease, and stroke.
The hormone released during the second half of the menstrual cycle by the corpus luteum in the ovary. Its function is to complete the preparation of the uterus for possible pregnancy.

A benign functional pituitary tumor that causes the pituitary gland to produce too much of the lactogenic hormone known as prolactin. Can cause infertility in women, erectile dysfunction in men, and can also impair vision.

definition: The process of physical changes by which a child's body becomes an adult body that is capable of reproducing. Marked by maturing of the genital organs, the development of secondary sex characteristics, and the first occurrence of menstruation in the female. In the United States the average age is 12 for girls and 11 for boys.

Abbreviated RAI; the oral administration of radioactive iodine to destroy thyroid cells. A nuclear medicine procedure, which disables at least part of the thyroid gland, used to treat thyroid cancer and chronic hyperthyroid disorders such as Graves' disease.

A large family of hormones derived from cholesterol. Examples produced by the body include cortisol, testosterone, and estrogen. Secreted by endocrine glands or artificially produced as medications to relieve swelling and inflammation in conditions such as asthma.
A steroid hormone secreted by the testicles and the adrenal cortex to stimulate the development of male secondary sex characteristics.
The surgical removal of the thymus gland.
A hormone that plays an important part in the immune system by stimulating the maturation of lymphocytes into T cells.
One of two primary thyroid hormones (the other is triiodothyronine) that regulate the rate of metabolism and affect the growth and rate of function of many other body systems.
The system whose primary function is to produce hormones that work together to maintain homeostasis. The hormones of the endocrine system affect almost every organ and cell in the body.
The process through which the body maintains a constant internal environment.

Chemical messengers that are secreted by endocrine glands directly into the bloodstream, enabling them to reach targeted cells and organs throughout the body. Each hormone has specialized functions in regulating the activities of specific cells, organs, or both.

Glands that produce hormones and do not have ducts. There are 13 major glands: one pituitary gland, one pineal gland, one thyroid gland, four parathyroid glands, one thymus, one pancreas, two adrenal glands, and two gonads.

Also known as the hypophysis; a pea-sized gland divided into the anterior and posterior lobes, which hang from a stalk-like structure located below the hypothalamus in the brain. Its primary function is to secrete hormones that control the activity of other endocrine glands.
The part of the nervous system that produces hormones that control many body functions. The pituitary gland acts in response to stimuli from neurohormones secreted by the hypothalamus.
Abbreviated ACTH; stimulates the growth and secretions of the adrenal cortex.
breakdown_text: adren/o: adrenal ; cortic/o: cortex ; trop: change ; -ic: pertaining to

definition: Also known as growth hormone (GH); regulates the growth of bone, muscle, and other body tissues.
breakdown_text: somat/o: body ; trop: change ; -ic: pertaining to

definition: Abbreviated LTH; also known as prolactin; stimulates and maintains the secretion of breast milk in the mother after childbirth.
breakdown_text: lact/o: milk ; gen: producing ; -ic: pertaining to

definition: Abbreviated MSH; increases the production of melanin in melanocytes, thereby causing darkening of skin pigmentation. Production usually increases during pregnancy.
Abbreviated TSH; stimulates the secretion of hormones by the thyroid gland. Produced by the anterior lobe of the pituitary gland, it controls the rate of secretion of thyroxine and triiodothyronine.

Also known as the pineal body; a very small endocrine gland located in the central portion of the brain. Takes its name from the Latin word for pinecone, referring to the shape of the gland. Its secretions influence the sleep–wakefulness cycle.
A hormone secreted by the pineal gland that influences the sleep–wakefulness portions of the circadian cycle.
The biological functions that occur within a 24-hour period.

A butterfly-shaped gland that lies on either side of the larynx, just below the thyroid cartilage. One of its primary functions is to regulate the body's metabolism; its secretions also influence growth and the functioning of the nervous system.
All of the processes involved in the body's use of nutrients, including the rate at which they are used.
One of the two primary thyroid hormones (the other is thyroxine) that regulate the rate of metabolism and affect the growth and rate of function of many other body systems.
Four glands, each about the size of a grain of rice, embedded in the posterior surface of the thyroid gland. Their primary function is to regulate calcium levels throughout the body.

Abbreviated PTH; works with the hormone calcitonin secreted by the thyroid gland to regulate the calcium levels in the blood and tissues. Higher-than-normal levels can increase calcium levels in the blood by mobilizing the release of calcium stored in bones and teeth.

A gland located near the midline in the anterior portion of the thoracic cavity, posterior to the sternum and slightly superior to the heart. Secretes a hormone that functions as part of the immune system, helping develop the body's immune system before birth and in childhood. Its function is greatly reduced after puberty, and it slowly turns into fatty tissue.
A feather-shaped organ located posterior to the stomach that functions as part of both the digestive and the endocrine systems.

The parts of the pancreas that have endocrine functions, which are to control the blood glucose levels and glucose metabolism throughout the body. An islet is a small isolated mass, or island, of one type of tissue within a larger mass of a different type.
Excess carbohydrate stored in the liver.

Also known as the suprarenals; glands located on top of each kidney. Each consists of an outer portion, the adrenal cortex, and the middle portion, the adrenal medulla. One of their primary functions is to control electrolyte levels within the body; they also help regulate metabolism and interact with the sympathetic nervous system in response to stress.
Sex hormones, primarily testosterone, secreted by the gonads, the adrenal cortex, and fat cells. Promote the development and maintenance of the male sex characteristics.

Abbreviated ALD; a corticosteroid that regulates the sodium and water levels in the body by increasing sodium reabsorption and potassium excretion by the kidneys. Reabsorption means returning a substance to the bloodstream.

Gamete-producing glands: ovaries in females and testicles in males. Secrete the hormones that are responsible for the development and maintenance of the secondary sex characteristics that develop during puberty.
Features that distinguish the two sexes but are not directly related to reproduction.
The early onset of the changes of puberty, usually before age 8 in girls and age 9 in boys. Precocious means exceptionally early in development or occurrence.
A reproductive cell: sperm in the male and ova (eggs) in the female.
Any hormone that stimulates the gonads.

Man-made substances that are chemically related to male sex hormones. Used in the treatment of hormone problems in men and to help the body replace muscle mass lost due to disease. Athletes may use them illegally to build muscle mass, a dangerous practice that can lead to lasting damage to the body.
A hormone produced in the gastrointestinal tract, sometimes referred to as the hunger hormone. A recent term created from the words Growth Hormone RELeasing with the suffix -in.

Hormones produced and released by neurons in the brain, rather than by the endocrine glands, and delivered to organs and tissues through the bloodstream. One example is neurohormones secreted by the hypothalamus that control the secretions of the pituitary gland.
A physician who specializes in diagnosing and treating diseases and malfunctions of the endocrine glands.
Abbreviated CDE; a health care professional qualified to teach people with diabetes how to manage their disease.
A condition in which the pituitary gland does not produce enough growth hormone. One of the causes of short stature, formerly known as dwarfism.
A condition in which an excess of prolactin causes the breasts to produce milk spontaneously, not due to childbirth.

Abbreviated SIADH; caused by the overproduction of the antidiuretic hormone ADH, often as a result of cancer or its treatment. High amounts of ADH keep the kidneys from excreting water, resulting in bloating and water retention that can dilute the blood, causing electrolyte imbalances, particularly hyponatremia (low levels of sodium).
A tumor of the pineal gland that can disrupt the production of melatonin. Can also cause insomnia by disrupting the circadian cycle.

The most common cancer of the endocrine system and the most rapidly increasing cancer in the United States. Has a high survival rate and affects significantly more women than men; commonly diagnosed between ages 20 and 55.

Also known as thyromegaly; an abnormal, benign enlargement of the thyroid gland that produces a swelling in the front of the neck. Usually occurs when the thyroid gland is not able to produce enough thyroid hormone to meet the body's needs, either due to Graves' disease, other medical conditions, or an iodine deficiency.
Lumps in the thyroid that can grow large enough to cause a goiter. Most are benign; however, some are malignant or produce too much thyroxine.

Also known as a thyrotoxic crisis; a relatively rare, life-threatening condition caused by exaggerated hyperthyroidism. Patients may complain of fever, chest pain, palpitations, shortness of breath, tremors, increased sweating, disorientation, and fatigue.

The overproduction of the parathyroid hormone, which causes the condition known as hypercalcemia. Can result from a disorder of the parathyroid gland or from a disorder elsewhere in the body, such as kidney failure. The opposite of hypoparathyroidism.
Caused by an insufficient or absent secretion of the parathyroid hormone. Causes hypocalcemia, and in severe cases leads to tetany. The opposite of hyperparathyroidism.
The condition of periodic, painful muscle spasms and tremors.
Characterized by abnormally low levels of calcium in the blood. The opposite of hypercalcemia.

definition: A tumor on the thymus. Myasthenia gravis can be characterized by an abnormally large thymus, with or without a thymoma.

An autoimmune insulin deficiency disorder caused by the destruction of pancreatic islet beta cells. Symptoms include polydipsia, polyphagia, polyuria, weight loss, blurred vision, extreme fatigue, and slow healing. Onset is often triggered by a viral infection. Treatment involves diet, exercise, and carefully regulated insulin replacement therapy administered by injection or insulin pump.
A small computerized device attached to the body designed to deliver insulin continuously into the subcutaneous tissue in the abdomen.

An insulin resistance disorder, in which insulin is being produced but the body does not use it effectively. Increasingly common in children and young adults with the rise of childhood obesity; obese adults are also at high risk. May be asymptomatic for years; treatment usually includes diet, exercise, and oral medications.
A condition in which insulin is being produced, but the body does not use it effectively. In an attempt to compensate for this lack of response, the body secretes more insulin.
Showing no symptoms.
A diet using the glycemic index to consume foods that will not raise the blood sugar more than necessary.
Medications that lower blood glucose by causing the pancreas to release more insulin or by increasing the body's sensitivity to insulin.
A medication that works within the cells to combat insulin resistance and to help insulin let blood glucose into the cells.

Abbreviated LADA; a condition in which type 1 diabetes develops in adults. Shares many of the characteristics of type 2 diabetes; however, autoimmune antibodies are present. Latent means present but not visible. Usually occurs in adults with a normal or low body weight and family history of type 1 diabetes; at least 10% of adult-onset diabetes is LADA, which can be misdiagnosed as type 2 diabetes.
Emergencies due to either too high or too low levels of blood glucose. Treatment depends on accurately diagnosing the cause.
Caused by very high blood glucose (hyperglycemia) or very low blood glucose (hypoglycemia) resulting in a stupor or coma. Causes a person to become unconscious and can be fatal if untreated.

Also known as insulin shock, diabetic shock, or insulin reaction; caused by very low blood glucose levels. Oral glucose, in the form of tablets, gel, or liquid, can be consumed to rapidly raise the blood sugar level; alternatively, glucagon can be administered via injection if the person is unable to take glucose by mouth.
The condition of excessive secretion of hormones by the sex glands. Can cause the early onset of puberty and increased libido.
breakdown_text: hyper-: excessive ; gonad: sex gland ; -ism: condition

definition: Characterized by the deficient secretion of hormones by the sex glands; more common than hypergonadism. Can lead to erectile dysfunction and low sperm count in men, and decreased libido and infertility in men and women. May also increase the risk of cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and other conditions.
breakdown_text: hypo-: deficient ; gonad: sex gland ; -ism: condition

definition: Abbreviated RAIU; uses radioactive iodine administered orally to measure thyroid function. The amount of radioactivity in the thyroid is measured 6 to 24 hours later using a handheld instrument called a gamma probe.
A diagnostic test to measure the circulating blood level of TSH. Used to detect abnormal thyroid activity resulting from excessive pituitary stimulation.
A form of nuclear medicine that measures thyroid function.

Abbreviated FBS; also known as a fasting plasma glucose test; measures the blood glucose levels after the patient has not eaten for 8 to 12 hours. Used to screen for diabetes as well as to monitor treatment of this condition.

Abbreviated OGTT; most commonly performed to diagnose type 2 or gestational diabetes. After fasting at least 8 hours, the patient has a baseline blood draw then drinks a liquid containing a high concentration of sugar, and the blood glucose level is tested after 1 hour and again after 2 hours.
Measures the current blood glucose level using a drop of blood and is often performed by the patient multiple times per day.

Abbreviated CGM; a method of tracking glucose levels 24 hours a day through a tiny sensor inserted under the skin on the abdomen or arm. The sensor measures the glucose levels in the cellular fluid just under the skin, with data continuously transmitted wirelessly to a smart phone or other device. An alert signals when glucose levels are too high or low.
Also known as HbA1c or A1c; a blood test that measures the average blood glucose level over the previous 3 to 4 months.

Abbreviated HGH; a synthetic version of the growth hormone that is administered to stimulate growth when the natural supply of growth hormone is insufficient for normal development. Sometimes abused by athletes in an attempt to increase lean body mass and decrease body fat.
The surgical removal of the pituitary gland, performed to treat cancerous or benign tumors. Performed through the nose or an opening in the skull.
A medication administered to slow the ability of the thyroid gland to produce thyroid hormones.
The surgical removal of one lobe of the thyroid gland. Also used to describe the removal of a lobe of the liver, brain, or lung.
The use of synthetic thyroid hormones, which are oral medications administered to replace lost thyroid function.

The surgical removal of all or part of the pancreas. A total pancreatectomy is performed to treat pancreatic cancer and also involves removing the spleen, gallbladder, common bile duct, and portions of the small intestine and stomach.

The synthetic equivalent of corticosteroids produced by the adrenal glands. Cortisone, and the synthetic corticosteroid prednisone, are administered to suppress inflammation and as an immunosuppressant.

Also known as an EpiPen; a device used to inject a measured dose of epinephrine. A synthetic version of epinephrine is used as a vasoconstrictor to cause the blood vessels to contract and is used to treat conditions such as allergic reactions, shock, and cardiac arrest.
